sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
June 2026 delivered a bifurcated global equity tape as the concentrated AI-driven mega-cap rally that powered markets through April and May encountered a trio of countervailing forces: a hawkish surprise from the Federal Reserve under Chair Kevin Warsh, a sector rotation away from semiconductors and technology toward cyclicals and small-caps, and geopolitical de-escalation that reshuffled relative performance between energy-heavy and tech-heavy markets. The S&P 500 slipped **-1.0%** to close at **7,499.36** — its first monthly decline after back-to-back gains of **+10.5%** in April and **+5.3%** in May — while the Nasdaq Composite fell **-2.8%** to **26,213.72** and the Dow Jones Industrial Average bucked the technology-led retreat with a **+2.7%** advance to **52,319.20**.

European equities outperformed their US counterparts, with the pan-European STOXX 600 climbing to a record high at **652.35** and Germany's DAX posting an all-time closing high, supported by the US-Iran ceasefire framework and eurozone inflation decelerating to **2.8%** year-on-year. APAC markets were mixed: Japan's Nikkei 225 extended its exceptional year-to-date leadership, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng and the Shanghai Composite traded cautiously amid BOJ policy uncertainty and persistent US-China trade friction.

The defining feature of June was rare market breadth. Seven of eleven S&P 500 sectors gained ground even as the headline index declined, and the Russell 2000 capped a historic first half with a **+22.93%** H1 2026 return — its best first half on record, running some **12 percentage points** ahead of the S&P 500. This broadening of leadership beyond mega-cap technology represents a potentially structural shift in the composition of equity returns heading into H2 2026.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
SpaceX IPO & Record H1 Equity Issuance -- The defining capital markets event of June 2026 was the June 12 Nasdaq listing of SpaceX (ticker: SPCX) — the largest initial public offering in recorded history — raising **$75 billion** at pricing with proceeds exceeding **$86 billion** after the greenshoe option was exercised. The IPO was priced at **$135** per share, implying a **$1.77 trillion** valuation at listing; SPCX closed its first trading session at **$161**, a **+19%** premium to the issue price, with over **207 million shares** trading in the first session — more dollar volume than SPY and QQQ combined. The debut briefly made Elon Musk the world's first US dollar trillionaire by equity market capitalization.

The SpaceX listing was the headline event in an extraordinary H1 for US equity capital markets: Alphabet concurrently raised approximately **$85 billion** in a landmark secondary equity offering, and total US IPO and secondary issuance topped **$250 billion** for the half — a new half-year record. Within weeks of its IPO, SpaceX returned to debt markets, raising **$25 billion** in a bond offering, underscoring management's ambition to deploy capital aggressively into its Starship and satellite broadband programs.

For portfolio allocators, the SpaceX IPO introduces a significant new competitor for capital within the aerospace and technology theme. With institutional demand absorbing this historic supply without material index disruption, the depth of investor risk appetite in mid-2026 is evident. Several additional large-cap unicorns are reportedly preparing H2 filings — a net equity supply dynamic that strategists must weigh carefully against an already elevated valuations environment.

US-Iran Ceasefire Framework & Crude Oil Supply Shock Reversal -- The most consequential commodity market development of June was the June 15 announcement of a preliminary US-Iran framework agreement extending a ceasefire and reopening the Strait of Hormuz to international shipping. The Strait — through which approximately 20% of global crude supply transits — had been disrupted by the Iran conflict that began earlier in 2026, sending Brent crude to an intraday 52-week high of **$120.88/bbl** on April 30. The US Treasury issued an immediate 60-day sanctions waiver on Iranian oil exports and petrochemical sales, enabling Iran to sell crude at full market rates for the first time in years and introducing a material new supply impulse.

Brent crude fell to approximately **$75/bbl** by June month-end — a decline of roughly **-37%** from its April peak — as markets began pricing the re-entry of Iranian barrels into the global supply pool. Goldman Sachs cut its Q4 2026 Brent forecast to **$80/bbl** from **$90/bbl** in response, and eurozone CPI fell to **2.8%** in June from **3.2%** in May — the lowest reading since the onset of the conflict — as lower energy costs worked through the supply chain. Global equity markets broadly rallied on the announcement, with European indices most immediately responsive given the region's acute sensitivity to energy import costs.

The medium-term macro implications are significant: the stagflationary impulse that had pressured consumer spending and corporate margins globally begins to reverse, providing a tailwind for growth assets. However, E&P companies and energy-sector earnings face meaningful H2 2026 guidance revision risk, and Saudi Arabia's fiscal breakeven requirements around **$80/bbl** suggest OPEC+ supply discipline will be tested if Iranian exports normalize faster than anticipated.

Warsh Hawkish Shock Reshapes the US Rates Outlook -- Kevin Warsh's inaugural FOMC meeting as Federal Reserve Chair on June 17 delivered a policy communication shock that upended consensus expectations for a dovish-leaning chair aligned with the administration. The committee held the federal funds rate steady at **3.50%–3.75%** for the fourth consecutive meeting — but nine of 18 FOMC participants penciled in at least one rate hike before year-end 2026, and the policy statement was dramatically shortened to approximately **130 words** (from over **300 in recent meetings**) as Warsh scrapped forward guidance entirely, stating it was "not well-suited to the current policy conjuncture."

Market reaction was immediate: the 2-year Treasury yield surged **14 basis points** on the announcement day — the largest single-session move on a Fed decision day in several years — while the Dow fell **410 points** and the S&P 500 declined **-1.06%** intraday. Warsh was unambiguous on price stability, stating that "the Fed will deliver price stability; the commitment is strong, unanimous, and unambiguous" — language that markets read as signaling openness to tightening in a way that the prior policy framework had systematically avoided. The 2-year yield subsequently settled near **4.07%**, approaching its highest level in over a year.

The strategic implications are far-reaching. A rate-hike restart — the first since the 2022–2023 cycle — was not discounted by equity or credit markets entering June. The repricing of the risk-free rate introduces incremental pressure on rate-sensitive sectors including real estate, utilities, and long-duration growth equities. Conversely, the banking sector stands to benefit from wider net interest margins if the hiking cycle materializes, consistent with the outperformance of financials in June.

AI Rotation & The Broadening of Market Leadership -- After powering global risk appetite for much of 2026, the narrow AI and semiconductor trade experienced its most significant correction in June. The Nasdaq Composite underperformed the S&P 500 by nearly **200 basis points** and the Dow by nearly **550 basis points** for the month, as investors differentiated between companies based on valuation, earnings visibility, and execution rather than rewarding AI positioning indiscriminately. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index posted its steepest weekly decline since March 2025 as profit-taking in extended names accelerated, a development that strategists characterized as healthy consolidation within a powerful secular theme rather than a reversal.

In parallel, market leadership broadened emphatically. Industrial companies, financial institutions, healthcare, and smaller-cap businesses outperformed as investors diversified beyond mega-cap technology. Equal-weight benchmarks outpaced cap-weighted equivalents, and the US flash composite PMI rose to **52.2** in June — with the manufacturing sub-index at **55.7**, its highest since May 2022 — providing fundamental validation for the cyclical rotation thesis. The Russell 2000 capped its best-ever first half at **+22.93%**, a performance trajectory that suggests small-cap outperformance may have structural rather than merely tactical drivers.

The rotation has material implications for active management and portfolio construction. If the broadening beyond mega-cap technology that emerged in June is sustained through H2 2026, it represents the evolution of the current bull market from a narrow, concentration-driven advance into a broad-based earnings expansion — a regime that historically supports active manager alpha and argues for reduced mega-cap concentration in benchmarks.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equity markets absorbed their first monthly drawdown of 2026 in June, with the S&P 500 declining **-1.0%** to close at **7,499.36** as the Federal Reserve's hawkish pivot under Chair Kevin Warsh compressed technology multiples and pushed Treasury yields higher. Despite the pullback, the index ended H1 2026 up **+9.6%** — an exceptional first-half performance by historical standards — while the Nasdaq Composite finished H1 up over **12%** before giving back **-2.8%** in June to close at **26,213.72**, weighed down by semiconductor profit-taking and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index's sharpest weekly decline since March 2025.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average delivered a starkly different outcome, gaining **+2.7%** to close at **52,319.20**, with industrials, financials, and healthcare leading blue-chip performance. The divergence between the Dow's **+2.7%** and the Nasdaq's **-2.8%** represents a **550 basis point** monthly spread — the widest gap between the two indices in several quarters — reflecting the most meaningful rotation within US equities since the market's early 2026 recovery. H1 2026 Dow performance of **+8.9%** was described as the index's best first half in five years. Small-cap performance was the headline story beneath the surface: the Russell 2000 delivered a **+22.93%** H1 2026 return — the best first half on record — running approximately **12 percentage points** ahead of the S&P 500.

Sector dispersion was unusually wide in June. Industrials led the S&P 500 for the month; healthcare, financials, and energy-adjacent value names also outperformed; communications services was the laggard. The historic SpaceX IPO on June 12 — which raised **$86 billion**, marking the largest public listing in history — and total H1 2026 equity issuance surpassing **$250 billion** underscored the exceptional depth of capital market demand even as the tape itself softened. Seven of eleven S&P 500 sectors posted gains for the month, confirming that June's index-level decline masked an unusually broad and constructive underlying picture.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities outperformed their US peers in June, with the pan-European STOXX 600 climbing to a record high at **652.35** and Germany's DAX printing an all-time closing high, as a confluence of geopolitical de-escalation and decelerating inflation provided a materially more constructive backdrop than the hawkish-Fed-driven turbulence weighing on US risk assets. The announcement of the US-Iran ceasefire framework on June 15 acted as a direct catalyst for European equities, which had been disproportionately exposed to the energy shock; the easing of Strait of Hormuz supply risk sent Brent crude toward **$75/bbl**, alleviating the single largest input-cost headwind facing European manufacturers, airlines, and logistics operators.

Eurozone inflation's decline to **2.8%** year-on-year in June from **3.2%** in May — the lowest reading since before the Iran conflict — reduced pressure on the ECB to pursue further tightening, lowering the cost of capital for European corporates and compressing sovereign spreads at the margin. Cyclical sectors led benchmark performance: industrials, financials, and defense names outperformed, as investors rotated toward value-oriented exposures with leverage to a stabilizing geopolitical environment. The FTSE 100 closed near approximately **10,679** (approx., verify before merging), with energy constituents tempering returns even as the broader UK market benefited from dollar strength amplifying the sterling value of multinational revenues.

European outperformance relative to the US in June reflects an external-tailwind-driven reprieve rather than a structural rerating of European earnings quality. Whether this persists into H2 will depend on the durability of the Iran ceasefire, ECB policy flexibility, and the degree to which Warsh's hawkish pivot tightens global financial conditions in ways that pressure European sovereign spreads and credit markets. Investors will scrutinize Q2 earnings season for evidence that European corporate margins can sustain themselves against higher financing costs and weaker Chinese demand — the two defining challenges facing the region heading into the second half.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asia-Pacific markets delivered a mixed outcome in June, with Japan continuing as the region's standout performer and China-linked markets trading under pressure from a combination of domestic macro headwinds and dollar-strength spillovers. Japan's Nikkei 225 extended its extraordinary 2026 run to approach a closing level near approximately **70,475** (approx., verify before merging) by month-end — representing a year-to-date gain approaching **+32%** — sustained by continued foreign institutional inflows, AI and semiconductor-related momentum among Japan-listed technology exporters, and a manufacturing sector benefiting from structural reshoring and supply-chain diversification flows. The Bank of Japan's deliberations over a further rate hike during June introduced intra-month volatility but did not derail the broader rally.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng closed June near approximately **22,881** (approx., verify before merging), under pressure from persistent stress in the domestic property sector, renewed US-China trade friction concerns, and dollar-strength headwinds weighing on Hong Kong dollar-pegged asset valuations. The Shanghai Composite ended the month near approximately **4,112** (approx., verify before merging), with targeted government stimulus measures and improving manufacturing PMI data providing a floor against more significant selling even as investor confidence in the pace of China's domestic consumption recovery remained fragile.

For APAC equities in H2 2026, the central tension is the interplay between a structurally stronger US dollar — driven by the Warsh Fed's hawkish pivot — and the region's diverse domestic growth trajectories. A Fed rate hike in H2, as the June dot plot implies, would create a classic emerging market policy dilemma between supporting growth and defending currency stability. Japan appears best positioned given its large-cap technology and industrial export mix; markets with higher dollar-liability exposure or elevated current account deficits face incrementally more challenging conditions if the dollar's bid strengthens further.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar firmed on a broad basis in June, with the DXY index closing the month at **101.341**, supported by the Warsh Fed's hawkish pivot, the removal of forward guidance, and nine of 18 FOMC participants projecting at least one rate hike before year-end 2026. The hawkish signal was particularly acute for the short end of the curve: 2-year Treasury yields surged **14 basis points** on the June 17 FOMC announcement day — their largest single-session move on a decision day in years — widening the US-global rate differential and attracting incremental capital flows into dollar-denominated assets. The DXY closing near **101.3** reflected a firm but not extreme dollar backdrop, consistent with a market that priced the hawkish signal as credible without fully discounting a multi-hike cycle.

EUR/USD weakened toward approximately **1.14** (approx., verify before merging) as the Fed-ECB rate divergence widened; despite lower eurozone energy prices providing a partial macro tailwind, the ECB's more cautious posture relative to the newly hawkish Fed left the euro vulnerable to continued dollar strength. GBP/USD held near approximately **1.33** (approx., verify before merging), as sterling derived marginal support from UK energy-import cost relief and a BOE maintaining a watchful stance on domestic inflation. USD/JPY remained elevated near approximately **158** (approx., verify before merging), with the Bank of Japan's rate-hike deliberations providing partial yen support against the dollar's broader advance; market participants flagged elevated Ministry of Finance intervention risk as the pair approached historically sensitive levels.

The DXY at **101.341** — approaching 13-month highs — carries material cross-asset implications. Dollar strength acts as a deflationary brake on dollar-denominated commodity prices, a headwind to US multinational earnings translations, and a tightening mechanism for EM economies with dollar-denominated debt burdens. Should the Warsh Fed proceed with a hike in H2 2026, the structural bid for the dollar is likely to intensify, adding a significant macro headwind to APAC and EM asset allocations that portfolio managers must price into H2 positioning.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
The commodity complex underwent its most significant repricing of 2026 in June as the US-Iran ceasefire framework fundamentally altered the near-term oil supply picture. Brent crude, which had reached a 52-week intraday high of **$120.88/bbl** on April 30 at the peak of the Strait of Hormuz disruption, fell to approximately **$75/bbl** by June month-end — a decline of roughly **-37%** from the April peak. The US Treasury's 60-day sanctions waiver on Iranian oil exports was announced within hours of the June 15 framework agreement, enabling Iran to sell crude at full market rates and introducing an incremental supply impulse that Goldman Sachs estimated would require a revision of its Q4 2026 Brent forecast to **$80/bbl** from the prior **$90/bbl**. WTI crude tracked Brent lower, settling near approximately **$72/bbl** (approx., verify before merging).

Gold demonstrated notable resilience, settling at **$4,008/oz** at June month-end — holding above the psychologically significant **$4,000** threshold — despite the twin headwinds of dollar strength and rising real yields that typically pressure the metal. Gold's ability to hold at these levels reflects the persistence of structural central bank accumulation and elevated investor demand for portfolio hedges in an environment characterized by significant monetary policy uncertainty, geopolitical transition, and a record-breaking equity capital markets cycle that has stretched valuations in risk assets.

Copper closed the month down **-2.1%** at **$6.254/lb**, reflecting dollar appreciation and softer-than-expected Chinese industrial demand data — a combination that tends to be most acutely negative for base metals given their sensitivity to global growth momentum and China's outsized role in industrial commodity consumption. The metal's retreat warrants monitoring: a sustained break below **$6.00/lb** would signal more meaningful industrial deceleration than consensus currently anticipates and would raise questions about the durability of the broadening cyclical recovery thesis that animated the equity rotation in June.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
US Treasuries experienced meaningful repricing in June as Kevin Warsh's inaugural FOMC meeting on June 17 delivered the most significant change in Federal Reserve policy communication since the pandemic era. The 2-year Treasury yield surged **14 basis points** on the announcement day alone — reacting to the removal of forward guidance, the hawkish dot-plot shift showing nine of 18 participants projecting a 2026 rate hike, and Warsh's unambiguous emphasis on the Fed's price-stability mandate. The 2-year settled near **4.07%** by June 26 — approaching its highest level in over a year — while the 10-year Treasury yield closed the month at approximately **4.38%**, establishing a month-end curve spread of approximately **+31 basis points** between the 10-year and 2-year.

The positive slope of the yield curve at month-end — with 10-year yields at **4.38%** and 2-year yields at **4.07%** — represents a normalization from the extended inversion that characterized much of 2024-2025 and is constructive for bank net interest margins. However, the level of the short end remains sufficiently elevated to exert pressure on rate-sensitive sectors: real estate investment trusts, utilities, and highly leveraged corporates face incremental refinancing headwinds, and any further move higher in the 2-year from **4.07%** would meaningfully tighten financial conditions in ways that equity market multiples have not yet fully discounted.

Credit spreads held broadly stable through June's rates volatility, a constructive signal suggesting markets view the potential hiking cycle as a calibrated response to above-target inflation rather than a harbinger of financial system stress. Investment-grade and high-yield spreads did not exhibit the widening that might be expected if the market were pricing recession risk alongside rate-hike risk. Heading into H2 2026, the US 10-year yield at **4.38%** sets a challenging but not prohibitive bar for equity valuations; the critical variable will be whether the Warsh Fed follows through on rate-hike signaling, which would force a systematic reassessment of terminal rate assumptions across the fixed income complex.
